Chapter 7: Lessons in Forgiveness and Letting Go
Forgiveness isn’t just one big decision—it’s a bunch of small choices we make, over and over, to finally let go of anger and disappointment.
For our friend, the path to forgiveness didn’t actually start with the First Lady. It started with herself. She had to give up the idea that she could’ve changed the outcome, or that maybe, if she’d just tried harder, things would be different today.
You know, most of us don’t realize just how much energy it takes to keep holding onto resentment. Our friend found herself drained, caught in those endless loops—replaying old hurts, searching for answers she was never going to find. But something shifted when she let herself really feel the weight of her grief. That’s when she started to find a little peace.
There were moments, too, when memories of happier times came floating back—a joke they once shared, a quiet moment when everything just clicked, the feeling of being truly seen by someone else. Those memories were bittersweet. Sure, they reminded her of what she’d lost, but they also brought back the warmth of real connection. Over time, she figured out how to hold onto those memories, without letting them take over her present.
Letting go doesn’t mean you forget. It’s more about accepting that not every relationship is meant to last forever. People change. Sometimes, the best thing you can do is wish someone well and keep moving forward. Our friend realized that forgiveness wasn’t something she was giving to the First Lady—it was something she was giving herself. It was her way of taking back control and finding her own peace.
As the months rolled into years, that sharp pain from betrayal faded away. What replaced it? A quiet kind of gratitude for the lessons she’d picked up along the way. She came out of it all with a deeper understanding of who she was, and a fresh commitment to living honestly and with compassion.
